- Cases: Slaughter-House Cases; Ward v. Maryland; United States v. Harris; United States v. Darby Lumber Co.
- Concepts: Fourteenth Amendment; Privileges or Immunities Clause; privileges and immunities; Commerce Clause; civil rights law; freedom of movement under United States law; Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938

Facts:
- Ward v. Maryland, 79 U.S. 418 (1871), was cited as a case in which the Court held that authority under the "privileges and immunities" clause was given to the states.
- The Slaughter-House Cases, 83 U.S. 36 (1873), was a pivotal early civil rights case.
- The Slaughter-House Cases held that the Fourteenth Amendment protects the privileges or immunities of citizenship of the United States, not the privileges and immunities of citizenship of a state.
- United States v. Harris, 106 U.S. 629 (1883), was cited as another case in which the Court consistently held that authority under the "privileges and immunities" clause was given to the states.
- United States v. Darby Lumber Co., 312 U.S. 100 (1941), upheld the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938.
- United States v. Darby Lumber Co. held that Congress had power under the Commerce Clause to regulate employment conditions.
